name: Reading contour lines
subject: Geography
example_problem: On a 1:50 000 extract with a 20 m contour interval, identify the river valley, the steepest slope and the spot height, and explain how contour spacing shows gradient.
prior_knowledge: Map symbols and height representation from Gr 8-9 mapwork

importance.summary: Mapwork is Question 3 on BOTH Geography papers, every year: 30/150 per paper in Gr 11 and Gr 12 (map skills & calculations 10, map interpretation 12, GIS 8) - contour reading is the entry point.

covered_by.topic: Consolidation of Grade 8 and 9 map skills
covered_by.subtopic: 1:50 000 topographic maps: natural and constructed features, height clues, contour patterns (river valleys, hills, mountains, ridges, spurs)

diagnostic.prompt: Contour lines drawn very close together indicate:
options: A steep slope - the fixed height gain happens over a short horizontal distance

diagnostic.prompt: In a river valley, the V-shaped bends in the contour lines point:
options: Uphill, toward the higher ground upstream

recap:
A contour line joins all points of equal height above sea level - walk along one and you neither climb nor descend. On a 1:50 000 topographic sheet the contour interval is typically 20 m: each line is 20 m higher or lower than its neighbours. Check the interval in the key before anything else. Three rules police every map: contours never cross (a point cannot have two heights), never simply end (they close into loops or run off the sheet), and every fourth or fifth line is a thicker, labelled index contour - your anchor for counting. A point between the 820 and 840 lines lies between those heights; a spot height (a dot with a number, like 913) pins a summit's exact altitude, which contours alone cannot give.

Spacing is gradient. Between neighbouring contours the land always rises the fixed interval; what varies is the horizontal distance walked to gain it. Lines far apart: the rise is spread over a long walk - gentle. Lines crowded: the same rise over a short distance - steep. Lines almost touching: a cliff. Even spacing means a uniform slope; wide-at-top, close-at-bottom is concave; close-at-top, wide-at-bottom is convex. To justify "steepest slope" in an exam, quote the evidence: the contours are closest together here, so the land rises 20 m over the shortest horizontal distance.

Valleys and spurs are the classic confusion pair, both showing bent contours. A valley's contours bend in a V pointing UPHILL, toward the upstream high ground - the line must detour up the low ground to keep its height - and a river often runs through it. A spur is high ground jutting between valleys: its bulge points DOWNHILL and never carries a river. When in doubt, read the heights on either side and ask which way is up. Confirm any river's direction two ways: the Vs point upstream, and the contour values crossing the river must decrease downstream - water never flows uphill.

Other signatures: closed rings with rising values - a hill; a stretched high band - a ridge; the dip between two summits - a saddle; almost no contours - a plain. Method for any question: read the interval, find the index contours, identify features by pattern, confirm with the printed heights, and answer by quoting spacing and values as evidence.

exit_check.prompt: Why can two contour lines never cross?
options: A single point cannot have two different heights
It would make the map untidy
Rivers would have nowhere to flow

exit_check.prompt: Contours crossing a river read 840, 820, 800 in the direction you trace it. You are tracing:
options: Downstream - heights must decrease in the direction of flow

exit_check.prompt: A bulge of contours pointing downhill, with no river, is a:
options: Spur - high ground jutting out between valleys

exit_check.prompt: What extra information does a spot height give that contours cannot?
options: The exact altitude of a point, not just a between-lines range
